## 🎯 Train a model from a DataFrame

The everyday supervised-ML loop — **without the boilerplate**. Point `train_model` at a DataFrame and a target column and it handles what normally takes 30+ lines by hand: it infers the task (classification vs regression), one-hot encodes categoricals, imputes missing values, splits train/test, fits the model, and prints the metrics. What you get back is a scikit-learn **Pipeline that takes RAW rows** — so you never have to reproduce the encoding at predict time.

| Stage | Helper | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Load | `read_athena` / `read_s3_csv` / `read_dynamodb` | pull a labelled table into a DataFrame |
| Train | `train_model(df, target=...)` | encode + split + fit + score, one call |
| Inspect | `model_info(model)` | features it expects, classes, hyperparameters |
| Score | `predict_batch(model, df)` | predictions (or probabilities) as a new column |
| Evaluate | `evaluate_model` / `plot_confusion_matrix` | metrics on a holdout + a confusion-matrix heatmap |
| Ship | `save_model` / `load_model` | persist to S3 as `.joblib`, reload anywhere |

```mermaid
graph LR
  D["Labelled DataFrame"] --> T["train_model"]
  T --> M["fitted Pipeline"]
  M --> I["model_info"]
  M --> P["predict_batch → scored rows"]
  M --> E["evaluate_model + plot_confusion_matrix"]
  M --> S["save_model → S3 (.joblib)"]
  S -. later .-> L["load_model ← S3"]
```

Replace the `<...>` placeholders with your table, target column, and bucket. `scikit-learn` is pre-installed — nothing to `pip install`.

# 1) Load your labelled data. Swap read_athena for read_s3_csv / read_dynamodb /
#    read_local depending on where it lives — they all return a DataFrame.
df = read_athena("SELECT * FROM <your_table> LIMIT 5000")
print(df.shape, "rows × cols")
df.head()

# 2) Train in ONE call. train_model infers the task from the target, one-hot encodes
#    categoricals, imputes, splits, fits, and prints held-out metrics.
#    Override anything you like:
#      task="classification"|"regression"   (auto-detected by default)
#      features=[...]                        (subset of columns; default = all but target)
#      estimator=<any sklearn estimator>     (default = a solid RandomForest/GBM)
#      n_estimators=, max_depth=, cv=, scale=
model = train_model(df, target="<target_column>")

# 3) Inspect the fitted model — the exact feature columns it expects (so you feed
#    the right RAW rows), the classes it predicts, and the chosen hyperparameters.
model_info(model)

# 4) Score the whole frame. predict_batch appends a column of predictions; the
#    Pipeline one-hots internally, so pass RAW rows (no manual get_dummies).
scored = predict_batch(model, df, output_col="prediction")
scored.head()

# 4b) For a CLASSIFIER, rank by likelihood instead of a hard 0/1 label — usually
#     what you actually want for a prioritized action list. proba=True appends the
#     class probability; sort to put the highest-risk rows on top.
ranked = predict_batch(model, df, output_col="score", proba=True)
ranked.sort_values("score", ascending=False).head(10)

# 4c) Evaluate on a held-out test set — evaluate_model returns the metrics dict
#     (accuracy/F1/AUC for classification, R²/MAE for regression; task auto-inferred).
#     Works on THIS model or any you load_model(...) later — not just a fresh train.
#     Split a quick holdout to score honestly (or pass your own X_test / y_test):
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
metrics = evaluate_model(model, test_df, test_df["<target_column>"])
metrics

# 4d) For a CLASSIFIER, see WHERE the errors land — plot_confusion_matrix renders a
#     labeled heatmap (rows = actual, cols = predicted). normalize=True shows the
#     per-true-class share, which reads better on imbalanced classes. (Skip for
#     regression.)
plot_confusion_matrix(model, test_df, test_df["<target_column>"], normalize=True)

# 5) Persist the trained model to S3 as a portable .joblib artifact, then reload it
#    (in this or any other notebook) with load_model — the shipped-model round trip.
uri = save_model(model, "<your-bucket>", "models/<name>.joblib")
print("saved:", uri)

# later / elsewhere:
# clf = load_model("<your-bucket>", "models/<name>.joblib")
# predict(clf, new_rows)
